name: Freya Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and still new to the sheet-folding machine at an industrial laundry. I left after secondary school and worked in a shop before the laundry hired me. I like a neat stack of clean hospital sheets; clearing a damp jam in the rollers leaves me flustered.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner cleans offices on shifts that change each week. Our grown children live elsewhere; we rent and have less than a month of expenses saved. My pay is low for a folder operator and there are few similar laundries nearby. I never use AI tools. I hope to stop paid work around 68 only if we can actually cover rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the laundry crew an office tool can sort the wash list, but it cannot tell whether a hospital sheet still smells of soap. We need a person checking the first bundle from the folding machine. I'd say that at the union lunch meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm 58 and a junior operator on the industrial sheet folder, still learning its feed rollers after years in other work. I left secondary school and the pay is low for this job. My partner cleans offices on short shifts; our grown children live elsewhere. We have under a month saved and few similar laundries nearby, so rent worries me already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep feeding the sheet folder and ask the lead to check my first stack each shift. At the union lunch meeting I'll bring the last three pay slips and ask about a fair rate for new operators. I never use AI tools. I'll keep the paper fault book I can explain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about bills, even if AI stays small. I hope to stop paid shifts around 68 if we can actually cover rent and food, but we cannot assume that yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the first bundle conceal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week the feeder doubled a sheet and hid a damp corner inside the stack. I opened the first bundle with the lead and sent it back through the dryer. A folded hospital sheet can look clean while a damp corner stays hidden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How steady is the cleaning income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office-cleaning rota changes every week, so I count only shifts actually posted. A rent increase would take most of our small reserve. My grown daughter visits on Sundays, but I do not expect her wages to pay our bills.

say: A **wash list** cannot detect a damp sheet hidden in a bundle.
The union should discuss **new-operator pay** alongside first-bundle checks.
think: My **junior rate** is low and I am still learning the folder.
Under one month saved and **variable cleaning shifts** make rent uncertain.
do: **Keep** feeding sheets and check first stacks with the lead.
**Bring** three pay slips to the union lunch meeting on operator rates.
feel: **Anxious** about current rent and low household income.
S0.quote: A folded hospital sheet can look clean while a damp corner stays hidden.
fieldNote: Freya is **58 and junior**, with secondary schooling and little reserve despite retirement being in sight.
Her **union pay request** and first-bundle check respond to present work; age 68 is only an affordable-income hope.

steps.text: Keep feeding sheet folder and check first stacks with lead
Bring three pay slips to union lunch meeting on new-operator rates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI may book laundry loads and answer customers before robots fold sheets. If management shortens a shift, I want the paid hours written down. A faster list will not dry a damp sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am still the learner on the folder, and a new schedule might take away one of my short paid shifts. My partner's office cleaning is already irregular. With less than a month saved, a lost shift would go straight through our rent budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the supervisor for the posted roster and compare it with the last three pay slips. I'll take any change to the union lunch meeting. If the laundry requires training on a new guarded feed roller and offers a paid trainer-led place on a stopped machine, I'll attend; I will not buy an AI class on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a real hours cut. I can learn a safe feed roller from a person standing beside it, but I cannot replace a missing shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would practical roller training include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trainer would have me lock the roller, clear a doubled sheet and restart with a test bundle. I want the guard closed before my hand goes near the feed. A slide show is not enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which roster number would you compare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The posted base hours matter, not a manager saying a busy week will make up for them. I would compare the rota with the rent date. If it is shorter, the union can ask why before we accept it.

say: **AI booking** may change laundry shifts before robots fold sheets.
Management should show **paid base hours** before a new target.
think: A short **folder shift** could be lost while I am still learning.
Our **thin reserve** and variable cleaning pay cannot bridge rent easily.
do: **Compare** posted roster with three actual pay slips.
**Bring** any paid-hour cut to the union meeting.
**Attend** required guarded roller course if paid trainer-led place offered.
feel: **Anxious** about realistic paid-hour loss and rent.
S1.quote: I can learn a safe feed roller from a person standing beside it, but I cannot replace a missing shift.
fieldNote: Her **technology resistance** still permits required paid guarded instruction with a trainer at a stopped roller.
She uses **actual roster hours** and union discussion rather than treating promised busy weeks as income.

steps.text: Compare posted folder roster with three pay slips

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the laundry crew thinking AI could plan loads by 2028, and capable robots around 2031 could feed and fold sheets. I would ask for written notice and paid work while the plant still has staff. Our union should bring every shift into that request.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 60 when thinking AI arrives and 63 when physical robots can do the folder work. I expect my junior shift could end, and my partner's short cleaning hours cannot cover rent and food. Under one month saved is no bridge. I already wake at night when the rota is thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll join the union meeting this month to ask for written notice and an offered paid course. We'll cancel our planned weekend trip to keep rent cash. If the plant offers a funded paid-time guarded practical place in linen quality checking, I'll enrol; if my folder shift ends, I'll apply for posted safe local laundry jobs only if base pay and travel cover rent, and after qualifying I'll apply for posted local quality roles under those terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I am too close to a possible stop date to spend years waiting for a second wage that may never come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must linen-quality training teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The quality course should show a wet corner, a torn hem and the safe way to stop a conveyor. I would practise with a trainer and a locked machine. I cannot pay fees or lose a day's wage for a demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make another laundry role possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fallback laundry job needs an actual local posting, a safe shift and enough pay after travel for our rent and food. If its start time clashes with my partner's cleaning rota, we need to count that too. A name on a jobs board is not an offer.

say: **2028 thinking AI** plans loads before robots fold around 2031.
The union should seek **written notice** and offered paid learning.
think: At **63**, I expect my junior folder shift could end.
Under one month saved and **short cleaning hours** cannot cover rent.
do: **Join** union request for written notice and paid learning.
**Enrol** in funded paid guarded quality training if place offered.
**Apply** to posted safe local laundry or qualified quality roles if displaced and net pay covers rent.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected wage loss and sleepless rent worry.
S2.quote: I am too close to a possible stop date to spend years waiting for a second wage that may never come.
fieldNote: Her **age 63 robot date** comes before any affordable retirement plan is confirmed, and she expects shift loss.
The **laundry fallback** and qualified quality application require real safe local posts with rent-covering net pay and workable shifts.

steps.text: Join union meeting for written notice and funded paid course
Enrol in linen quality if funded paid guarded practical place offered
Apply for posted safe local laundry if displaced, net pay and cleaning rota fit
Apply for posted safe local quality if qualified, displaced, net pay and cleaning rota fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI could book laundry loads in 2031, and capable robots fold sheets around 2034. At 63 and then 66, I need paid years to decide whether retirement is possible. A course brochure does not settle the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 when robots can do the physical folding. I might still need both wages because we have saved so little. If I can keep working to 68, the extra pay might help, but I cannot decide to stop until we have counted income and costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the folder shift and add a small amount from each full-pay week to our reserve after rent. At the union meeting I'll ask for paid time and covered fees for a practical linen-inspection course. If a guarded trainer place is offered, I'll attend; after qualifying, if folding hours fall, I'll apply to posted safe local inspection only if the net wage and travel work for our household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about today's rent and a possible lost shift at 66. A little more warning helps only if the paid weeks arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would linen inspection test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The practical test should make me spot a damp bundle and stop a jammed feed before signing a load. A trainer must watch me do both on a guarded machine. I would not spend the small reserve on tuition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the posting need to pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the posted base wage and how long it takes to travel there. If the wage after travel does not meet rent and food, I would keep looking. Turning 66 will not pay our rent.

We need **paid working years** to judge retirement affordability.
think: At **66**, I may still need both wages because the rent keeps arriving each month.
Our **small reserve** cannot replace a full working year or turn a course brochure into a paid place.
do: **Save** new money from full weeks after rent.
**Attend** funded paid guarded linen inspection if place offered.
**Apply** for posted safe local inspection if qualified, hours fall and net pay covers rent.
feel: **Anxious** about current rent and future folder hours.
S3.quote: Turning 66 will not pay our rent.
fieldNote: Her **new deposits** come from full paid weeks after rent, while age 68 remains an affordability goal.

steps.text: Save new money from full folder wages after rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI could plan wash loads by 2036, and capable robots could fold sheets around 2039. I would be 68 at the first date. If work income still pays our rent, I will not call that a retirement plan just because I have reached an age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68, I hope we can stop paid shifts if our actual household income covers rent and food; I do not know yet. If it does not, I may still be working when robots reach the folder at 71. Less than a month saved today makes even a decade feel uncertain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the folding job while it is offered and save a little from full paid weeks after rent. I'll ask for a written estimate of our retirement income and housing costs, then decide whether stopping around 68 is affordable. If I am still employed after 2036 and folder hours fall, I'll apply for posted safe local linen work only where net pay and travel cover the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about current money, with time to gather real figures. Ten years does not turn a thin bank balance into income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What figures would make stopping possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare any actual retirement income we can document with rent, food and medicines. If the total is short, I keep taking shifts rather than announce a leaving date. I would ask someone at the household budget service to check my arithmetic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a later job need to offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need the posted base rate, safe duties and a route I can travel reliably. If a laundry job pays less after travel than the rent needs, I would not apply. I would also ask my partner whether the cleaning rota could fit the shift.

Stopping paid work at **68** needs actual affordable income.
think: At **68**, retirement may be affordable or not.
Our **thin reserve** today makes continued wages possible after 2036.
do: **Save** new money from full paid weeks after rent.
**Check** documented retirement income against rent and food before deciding.
**Apply** if still employed and hours fall, only for posted safe local net pay.
feel: **Anxious** about current rent despite a longer planning window.
S4.quote: Ten years does not turn a thin bank balance into income.
fieldNote: The **retirement enquiry** gathers numbers; no early exit or pension payment is assumed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could end my folder shift at 63 before I have enough income to stop working. Written notice, a funded paid practical place and posted safe local work with enough net pay would help. I need a real household budget before any retirement date.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who opens the first folded bundle after a robot starts the machine. A wet hospital sheet can be hidden inside a perfect stack.

headlineQuote: A wet hospital sheet can be hidden inside a perfect stack.
portrait: **Freya**, 58, is a junior laundry-folder operator with secondary schooling and no AI use.
She and her office-cleaner partner have **grown children**, rent, low pay, under a month saved and few nearby laundries.
Her **progressive outlook** takes wage and notice concerns to union meetings, while she prefers guarded in-person instruction.
Fast robots leave her **alarmed** about income at 63; stopping around 68 depends on documented rent-covering household income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable laundry robots around 2031, ending paid folder work before retirement is affordable.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, funded paid practical training and posted safe local work with sufficient net pay would help.
